name: Bianca Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run three CNC mills at a precision machining shop that makes brackets and housings for aircraft parts. CNC means the machine cuts metal from a programme, so my job is loading the aluminium blocks, setting the zero point, watching the first part come off and measuring it with a micrometer. I'm not allowed to edit the programmes yet, that's for the programmers upstairs, and I'm still slow at setups. Last week I measured a bore wrong and we scrapped six parts, which hurt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a good day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A good day is when I catch a problem before the machine does, like hearing the tool start to chatter and stopping it before it snaps. I use an AI chat app basically every day, on my break, asking it things like why a tool would chatter at a certain speed, and then I check it with Dmitri, our lead. Bad days are long, the shop's cold in winter, and some of the older guys still call me the new girl after two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a bit disappointing. I'd post something like, all that noise and it's a slightly better search engine. I genuinely use it every day, so I'd miss the hype a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing, I keep learning the machines the slow way. Honestly I'd feel a bit relieved for the older guys, they'd stop worrying about being replaced. I'd still want to move upstairs to programming in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep putting money into my index fund, a few hundred a month like now, and ask Dmitri if I can shadow the programmers on Friday afternoons. I'd keep using the AI app to study for the CAM software, that's the programme that turns drawings into tool paths. Nothing urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a little bored. I like change, so no change is a bit dull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be relieved for the older guys. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerhard, mostly. He's been on the old manual lathe for twenty-five years and he's terrified of the new five-axis machine. He calls me in to press buttons for him, and then pretends he was testing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the index fund. How did you end up with savings like that at twenty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worked a lot of overtime the first two years and I share a flat with my friend Leila, so the rent is low. My aunt told me to put money in a fund and forget about it, so I did. It's about a year's worth of spending now, which feels unreal.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit disappointing, all that noise for a slightly better search engine. She uses AI daily, so she'd miss the hype a little.
S0.think: It changes nothing for her and she keeps learning machines the slow way. She'd be relieved for older colleagues and still plans to move upstairs into programming.
S0.do: Keeps paying a few hundred a month into her index fund and asks to shadow the programmers on Friday afternoons. Keeps using an AI app to study for the CAM software.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly bored, because she enjoys change.
S0.quote: He calls me in to press buttons for him, and then pretends he was testing me.
S0.fieldNote: She is the rare operator who'd find a plateau a let-down. Her plan to move into programming exists with or without AI. Strong savings came from overtime, shared rent and an aunt's advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs managing properly, with unions and government involved, so the gains don't just go to the owners. Retraining should be free and paid while you do it. I'd be the one at work explaining what the new software actually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this one's good for me. The parts of my job that'll go are loading and measuring, and I'd rather be programming or looking after robots anyway. My worry is for people like Gerhard, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the shop to put me forward for the robot cell training as soon as they buy one, and I'd do an evening course in CAM programming, about two nights a week. I'd use AI tools to learn faster. I'd also join the union properly, because we don't really have one in the shop and someone should start it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. And a bit guilty about being excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start a union. Is that realistic in a small shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're about forty people, so it's not huge, but it's enough to need one. There's a metalworkers' union in the region, and Gerhard was a member at his old job. If I could get him and two or three others, I think the rest would follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you feel guilty about being excited. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the same thing that's fun for me is scary for Gerhard and for my cousin who works on a car plant assembly line. It's easy to be excited when you're twenty-seven, with a year of savings and no kids. I try to keep that in mind.

S1.say: I'd say this needs managing with unions and government so gains don't just go to owners, with free, paid retraining. She'd be the one at work explaining the new software.
S1.think: Privately she thinks it's good for her, since the loading and measuring she does would go and she'd rather program or run robots. Her worry is for colleagues like Gerhard.
S1.do: Asks to be first in line for robot cell training and takes a CAM programming evening course two nights a week. Uses AI tools to learn faster and tries to start a union branch in the forty-person shop.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with a twinge of guilt about the excitement.
S1.quote: It's easy to be excited when you're twenty-seven, with a year of savings and no kids.
S1.fieldNote: Her progressive views and personal ease sit side by side without much strain: she'd push for collective protection she doesn't think she needs. She is self-aware about her privilege. She'd organise the shop rather than just retrain herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is reckless. Nobody voted for full AGI in two years, and governments should have slowed it down or at least had the money ready to support people. I'd be pushing hard for a universal basic income, online and in the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared, even me. All my plans, programming, robot cells, assume there's a next step, and if AI can programme and robots can fix robots, there's no next step. My savings would buy me a year or so, but a year to do what?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as long as the shop exists, and I'd try to get onto the team that installs and tests the new systems, because someone has to be there at the start. I'd move my fund into cash so a crash doesn't wipe it. I'd join every campaign for a basic income and bring Leila along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, I'd still be doing things, but my stomach would be tight all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a year to do what. What would you actually do with that year, if the shop closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd volunteer, maybe help older workers like Gerhard figure out benefits and forms, using AI to help them. It sounds strange, but I'd want to be useful. And I'd probably travel for a month, because when else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said the changes would be good for you. Now you're anxious. What's the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the slower one, there's a ladder and I'm good at climbing it. Here someone's taken the ladder away. Being adaptable only helps if there's somewhere to adapt to.

S2.say: I'd say this is reckless and nobody voted for it; governments should have slowed it or had money ready. She'd push hard for a universal basic income online and in the street.
S2.think: Even she would be scared, because her plans assume a next step and AGI removes it. Her savings buy about a year, but she doesn't know what the year is for.
S2.do: Keeps working while the shop exists and tries to join the team installing new systems. Moves her fund into cash to protect it from a crash and joins basic income campaigns, bringing her flatmate along.
S2.feel: Anxious with a tight stomach, but still active rather than frozen.
S2.quote: Being adaptable only helps if there's somewhere to adapt to.
S2.fieldNote: This is the scenario where her adaptability stops being a shield, and she names that herself. She would still act, but her actions shift from climbing to protecting and helping others. Her instinct with spare time is to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it's enough to put a basic income and free retraining in place if politicians want to. I'd be organising at work and talking about it online. I'd say the people who build these systems should pay for the transition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd likely get my programming role first, maybe even work on the robot cells for a few years. I'd be one of the people setting up the machines that replace us, which is weird. I'd be okay for a while, then probably in the same place as everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the CAM course in year one and push to be the robot cell operator in year two. In years three and four I'd save hard and move some money into broader investments, maybe property with my brother. And I'd get the union in the shop going, because it'd matter more by year five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's time to do things, which helps, but I know where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be setting up the machines that replace you. How would that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly some days. I'd tell myself someone's going to do it, and better me than a contractor who doesn't know Gerhard's name. I'd make sure the cell is set up so the old guys can at least supervise it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned property with your brother. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a plumber and he's been on at me to buy a small house with him and rent half of it out. I always said I'd rather keep my money liquid. But if jobs are going, rent from a real building starts to sound sensible.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but enough for a basic income and free retraining if politicians want it. The people who build these systems should pay for the transition.
S3.think: She'd likely get her programming role and work on robot cells for a few years, essentially setting up her own replacement. She expects to be fine for a while, then in the same place as everyone.
S3.do: Finishes the CAM course in year one and pushes for the robot cell role in year two. Saves hard in years three and four, considers buying a rental property with her plumber brother and builds the shop union.
S3.feel: Uneasy, helped by having time but aware of the end point.
S3.quote: I'd tell myself someone's going to do it, and better me than a contractor who doesn't know Gerhard's name.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her climb a few rungs before the end, which takes her down from anxious to uneasy. She shows a real moral tension about building her own replacement. Property only becomes appealing once jobs look shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to get this right. A shorter working week, a guaranteed income, free training and public ownership of some of the AI, so the gains are shared. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven and probably a programmer, maybe running the automation in the shop. I'd have had a good decade. Then it ends for me as well, and I'm not sure what I'd want to do with my life without work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd climb the ladder as fast as I can for the first five years, programming then automation, and keep putting money into the fund and maybe the house with my brother. Around year six I'd start thinking about what I'd do if work stopped, maybe teaching people to make things by hand, as a hobby that might become something. I'd be active in politics the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly curious. I'd want to see what the world looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure what you'd do without work. Is that a worry or an opportunity for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I like the feeling of a good part coming off the machine, measuring it and it's dead on. If a robot does that, I'd want to find that feeling somewhere else, maybe a pottery wheel, maybe fixing old motorbikes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're progressive and you want public ownership. But you also invest in a fund. Does that clash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I'd say I'm being realistic, if the world's run by whoever owns the robots, I want a tiny piece of it while also voting for everyone to get a piece. I know it sounds like having it both ways.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to get it right: a shorter week, a guaranteed income, free training and public ownership of some AI. She'd be loud about it.
S4.think: She expects a good decade climbing into programming and automation, then the end arrives for her too. She's unsure what she'd want from life without work.
S4.do: Climbs from programming to automation over the first five years while investing in her fund and possibly a house with her brother. From around year six explores teaching hand skills or crafts, and stays politically active throughout.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly curious about what the world would look like.
S4.quote: I want a tiny piece of it while also voting for everyone to get a piece.
S4.fieldNote: She admits the tension between her investing and her call for public ownership, and doesn't hide from it. What she'd miss is the satisfaction of a part measured dead on, not the wage. More time makes her curious rather than calm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no ladder to climb. What would help is a basic income that arrives automatically, plus some kind of community workshop where people can still make things with their hands and teach each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the older guys much. Everyone asks people my age because we're the future, but the guys in their fifties who've spent thirty years on a lathe have the most to lose and the least time to adjust. I'd ask them what they need, then do that.

headlineQuote: In the slower one, there's a ladder and I'm good at climbing it. Here someone's taken the ladder away.
portrait: Bianca Usman is a 27-year-old junior CNC operator at a precision machining shop making aircraft brackets, still slow at setups but eager to move into programming. She uses AI daily, shares a flat with a friend and has about a year of spending in an index fund. She's progressive and would try to start a union in her forty-person shop. She's calm about a plateau and steady change, which she sees as a ladder to climb, but anxious if AGI lands in two years and the ladder disappears. With five or ten years she becomes uneasy and curious, while admitting the clash between her investing and her call for shared ownership.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no ladder left for her to climb.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income that arrives automatically, and community workshops where people can keep making things with their hands and teach each other.
